Creation is handed to the domain via Subscription.start(this.subscriptions.nextId(), customerId, plan, seats)
Saving goes through the port: await this.subscriptions.save(subscription), with no storage details
The result is mapped to the application DTO via summarise(subscription, plan)

parsedVerdict.reasoning: StartSubscription.execute works the way an application use case should. It checks the incoming parameters, looks up the plan through the PlanCatalog port, and checks preconditions through the SubscriptionRepository port. It then hands creation to the domain factory Subscription.start, saves the result through the port, and maps it to an application DTO with summarise. There is no persistence code here (no SQL or ORM), no transport code (no HTTP request or response handling) and no framework code. ExecuteContextDto is an application-level input DTO. One judgement call: the seat-count check (a whole number, at least one) could arguably sit in Subscription.start as a domain invariant. At the use-case boundary, though, it is reasonable input validation. The check that the customer doesn't already have this plan needs repository data, so it is legitimate application orchestration. I found no responsibility that clearly belongs to a different kind of layer.
